intro.t: Practice test. Listening. In this test, you will hear four recordings and answer questions on what you hear. You will have time to read the instructions and questions before each recording, and time to check your work. Each recording will be played once only.

segments.t: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a company that organises cycle tours. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
There is an example at the beginning of the conversation. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6.
Good morning, Greenway Cycle Tours, Daniel speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm ringing about your guided tours. I'm organising a day out for some friends and family, and I saw on your website that you do a few different routes.
That's right. At the moment we've got three: the Coastal Loop, the Forest Trail and the Riverside Tour. Did you have one in mind?
Well, I was going to ask about the Forest Trail, but a friend told me it's quite hilly, and some of our group haven't been on a bike for years. So I think the Riverside Tour would suit us better.
Good choice. It's almost completely flat, and it's our most popular route.
Great.
Let me take a few details. Can I have your name, please?
Yes, it's Sophie Hargreaves.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Sure. It's H, A, R, G, R, E, A, V, E, S.
Thank you. And is there a phone number we can reach you on?
My mobile's best. It's oh seven seven three four, double five eight, two nine one.
Let me just read that back. Oh seven seven three four, five five eight, two nine one.
That's it.
Lovely. Now, when were you thinking of going?
We'd like to go on a Sunday in May. I was hoping for the ninth.
Let me check. I'm afraid the ninth is fully booked. It's a holiday weekend, so it gets very busy. The following Sunday, the sixteenth, is still wide open, though.
The sixteenth. Yes, that should be fine. Everyone's free that weekend too.
Great, I'll put you down for the sixteenth. And how many of you will there be?
When I first asked around, twelve people said yes, but two of my cousins have since told me they can't make it. So it'll be ten.
Ten. OK. Now, all our tours include bike hire. Most people go for our standard hybrid bikes, but we also have mountain bikes and electric bikes.
What's the difference in price?
The electric ones cost a little more, but I'd recommend them if some of your group are worried about keeping up.
I think that would really help my parents. Actually, could we just have electric bikes for everyone? Then nobody gets left behind.
Of course, that's no problem at all.
And where does the tour start?

The meeting point used to be in front of the town museum, but there's building work going on there at the moment, so we've moved it. We now meet outside the library on Market Street. It's opposite the post office.
Oh yes, I know it.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
Could you tell me about the cost?

Of course. The standard price for the Riverside Tour is forty-two pounds per person, but you'll get our group rate, which applies to groups of eight or more. That brings it down to thirty-five pounds each.
That's good. And does that include the electric bikes?
It does, yes. The group rate covers any type of bike.
Excellent. What about food? Is there somewhere to stop for lunch?

There's a pub halfway along the route, but it gets very crowded on Sundays. What a lot of groups do instead is order one of our picnic lunches. They're made for us by a local bakery, and the sandwiches and cakes are fantastic. It's an extra six pounds per person.
That sounds lovely. I'll talk to the others, but I'm fairly sure we'll want that.
Just let us know a few days before.
Will do. Is there anything we need to bring?

Well, we provide helmets and locks, and there's a map on every bike. But the weather can change very quickly by the river, so everyone should bring a waterproof jacket. Some sun cream is a good idea too, and maybe a small bag for personal things.
OK, I'll pass that on.
And one last question, if you don't mind. We like to know how people heard about us. Was it from our website?

Well, I did look at the website, but that's not how I first found out about you. I thought it was a colleague who mentioned you, but actually, now I think about it, it was a podcast. They were talking about cycling holidays in the region, and your company came up.
Oh, that's nice to hear. Right, I'll send you a confirmation by text this afternoon.
Thank you so much.
That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
Part 2. You will hear the manager of a public park talking to a group of local residents. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming along tonight. My name's Karen Webb, and I'm the manager here at Ashford Park. As most of you know, the park reopened to the public last month after being closed for almost two years, and this evening I'd like to tell you a bit about what's changed, and how you can get involved.

First of all, I'd like to clear up a misunderstanding. A lot of people seem to think that we closed the park in order to create the new lake. In fact, the lake had been part of our plans for a long time, but it was never urgent. It's also true that some of the oldest trees needed attention, but our tree surgeons dealt with those in a matter of weeks. No, the real problem was the storm we had two winters ago. Heavy rain flooded the whole lower half of the park, and the water destroyed most of the old drainage system. Until that had been completely replaced, it simply wasn't safe to let the public back in.

Now, the lake itself. Some of you may have seen photographs in the local paper of people paddling around in kayaks. Those were taken on our opening day, when a canoe club from the town gave a demonstration. I'm afraid the lake isn't actually open for boating yet. We still need to finish building the jetty, and that won't be ready until next spring. Once it is, we'll be hiring out rowing boats every weekend. And just so there's no confusion, swimming will never be allowed in the lake. The water is surprisingly deep in places.

We're also looking for more volunteers. We've been very lucky with tree planting. In fact, last autumn we had more volunteers than trees! And the café is run by a local charity, which has its own staff. What we really need are people who can lead guided walks for schools and visitors. You don't need to be an expert on plants or wildlife; we'll give you all the training you need.

One last practical point. In the summer, the gates will open at seven in the morning and close at nine in the evening, as before. In the winter, though, we'll be closing at five o'clock. Some people have suggested that this is to save money, but that isn't the case. It's simply that the new paths don't have any lighting yet, and it isn't safe to walk around in the dark. Once lights have been installed, we'll look at the times again.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

Now, if you look at the map I've given you, I'll show you where everything is. We're starting at the main entrance on Station Road, at the bottom of the map. As you come through the gates, the building immediately on your right is the visitor centre. That's where you'll find toilets and information, and it's also where you can book a guided walk. The building opposite it, on your left as you come in, is our office, which unfortunately isn't open to the public.

If you carry straight on along the main path towards the lake, you'll pass the children's play area. It's on your right, about halfway between the entrance and the lake. A lot of parents have told us they like the fact that it's well away from the road.

Now, if, instead of going straight on, you take the path that turns left just after the entrance, it'll take you to the large open area on the western side of the park. That's our new wildflower meadow. It's at its best in June and July, and we ask everyone to keep to the mown paths, so that the flowers aren't damaged.

If you carry on along that path, it'll bring you up to the north-west corner of the park, which is where we've put the picnic area. There are tables there and a couple of barbecue stands, and it gets the sun for most of the afternoon.

From there, the path runs along the top of the lake. Halfway along the north shore, you'll see the boathouse. It's still being built at the moment, but that's where the rowing boats will be kept once the jetty is ready.

And finally, for any bird lovers here tonight, we've built a new bird hide. If you go past the boathouse and follow the path round to the eastern side of the lake, you'll find the hide right at the water's edge, between the lake and the river. It's a wonderful place to watch herons early in the morning. Oh, and you may notice a small building in the south-east corner of the park, down near the river. That's just a storage shed for our maintenance equipment, so it isn't open to visitors.
Right, does anyone have any questions?
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
Part 3. You will hear two business students, Amira and Ben, discussing a case study they are writing for their marketing course. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
Hi, Amira. Sorry I'm late. The bus took forever.
No problem. I've just been rereading our notes on Treadwell. Shall we start with the history section?
Sure. I have to say, I found the background research really interesting. There were a couple of things I didn't expect at all.

Me too. I mean, I already knew the founders didn't come from the shoe industry. That's mentioned in pretty much every article about them. But I had no idea the company began by repairing old trainers and selling them on.
I know! Before they'd made a single pair of their own. And the other thing that surprised me was how they paid for their first factory. I'd always assumed they'd taken out a big bank loan.
But it was the customers who funded it, through that online campaign.
Exactly. Thousands of people paid in advance for shoes that didn't even exist yet.
What about the story that their first shoe was a failure? Someone in our seminar group mentioned it.

That's just a rumour, as far as I can tell. The first model actually sold out in a few weeks. And people also say they've never paid for advertising, but that's not quite right either. They did spend money on social media adverts in their first year. It's just that these days they rely mostly on word of mouth.
OK. Now, Doctor Patel's feedback on our draft. Shall we go through it section by section?
Good idea. She said the introduction was far too long.
She did. I think we could get it down to half a page without losing anything important. I did wonder about opening with a quotation from one of the founders.
Hmm, I'd rather save the quotation for the company history. It fits better there, because it explains why they started the business in the first place.
Fair enough. So the history section gets the quotation, and we cut the introduction down.
Right. Then there's the competitor analysis.
That's the one with the huge table comparing prices.
It's nearly two pages long. Doctor Patel suggested putting the full table at the end, in an appendix, and just summarising the main points in the text.
That makes sense. I was going to suggest adding some figures on market share, but honestly, I think we've got more than enough numbers already.
Agreed. And what about the recommendations?
Well, Doctor Patel was quite positive about those. I did think about changing the order, so that the cheapest recommendation comes first.
I don't know. I think the order is logical as it is. It goes from short term to long term.
True. OK, let's not touch that section, then.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
By the way, I've been thinking about how we explain why we chose Treadwell in the first place. Should we say it's because they've grown so fast?

Their growth is impressive, but lots of companies have grown quickly. For me, what really decided it was how much material is available. Interviews with the founders, annual reports, even their sustainability audits are published online.
That's true. And I suppose we can't say it's because I've got contacts there.
Your cousin?
Yes. It turns out she doesn't work for Treadwell at all. She works for one of their competitors!
Oh dear. Well, that might be useful in a different way. Anyway, in the analysis, we need to identify the company's main weakness. What do you think?

Well, people often criticise their prices, but I don't think that's the real issue. Their customers seem perfectly happy to pay more for sustainable products. And they've been quite cautious about expanding abroad, so that's not a problem either. What worries me is that almost eighty per cent of their sales come from just one model, the Trail Runner. If that goes out of fashion, they're in serious trouble.

Good point. That leads nicely into our recommendations. I don't think opening more shops of their own is realistic. The rent in city centres is enormous. And working with a celebrity designer would go against their whole image.
So what would you suggest?

I think they should develop a range of children's shoes. Parents care a lot about sustainability, and because children's feet grow so quickly, Treadwell could offer a scheme where families send back shoes that are too small, so they can be recycled.
I like that. It fits their brand perfectly.
So what's next? Should we send a short questionnaire to some of their customers?
I'd love to, but there isn't time before the deadline. We could ask Doctor Patel for advice about the structure, but she's away until Friday.
Then I think we should just divide up what's left. Why don't you write the recommendations, and I'll put together the appendix?
Perfect. Let's meet again on Monday to put it all together.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
Part 4. You will hear a lecture about a branch of ecology. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to introduce a relatively new field of research known as soundscape ecology.

Traditionally, ecologists have studied habitats mainly by looking at them: counting the number of species in an area, for example, or measuring how quickly plants grow. Soundscape ecology takes a different approach. It studies the relationship between living organisms and their acoustic environment. In other words, all the sounds that surround them.

The discipline itself is quite young, but its roots go back several decades. Interestingly, many of the first people to make long recordings of natural soundscapes weren't scientists at all. They were musicians, who were originally searching for unusual sounds to use in their compositions. Over time, some of them noticed that their recordings contained valuable information about the condition of the habitats they'd visited, and that some places they had recorded years earlier had become noticeably quieter.

Researchers usually divide a soundscape into three components. The first is known as biophony, which means all the sounds produced by living organisms: birdsong, the calls of frogs, the buzzing of insects, and so on. The second is geophony, that is, natural sounds that don't come from living things. Wind is the most obvious example. But in polar regions, one of the most dramatic sounds is the cracking of ice as the temperature changes. The third component is anthrophony: the sounds produced by human activity. Some of this comes from machinery or aircraft, but by far the largest source, in most places, is traffic on the roads.

So how is this kind of research actually carried out? The basic equipment is surprisingly simple: a weatherproof digital recorder, which is attached to a tree or a post. What's very different from traditional fieldwork is the timescale. Rather than recording for an hour or two, researchers typically leave these devices in place for several months, programmed to switch on at regular intervals. As you can imagine, this produces an enormous amount of data, far more than anyone could ever listen to. So researchers use computer software to analyse it. One common result of this analysis is what's called an acoustic index. This is a single number that summarises how varied and complex the sounds in a recording are, and it's increasingly being used as an indicator of the overall health of an ecosystem. Generally speaking, a healthy forest is a noisy forest, full of many different voices.

Let's turn now to some of the findings. One area that's received a great deal of attention is the effect of human noise on wildlife. Many animals depend on sound to attract a mate or to warn others of danger, so noise can be a serious problem for them. Studies in several European cities have found that some birds now sing at a higher pitch than birds of the same species living in the countryside. The explanation seems to be that traffic noise is mostly low in frequency, so it tends to drown out low notes, while higher songs can still be heard. Other species have changed the timing of their calls instead. Certain frogs living close to busy roads appear to wait for gaps in the traffic noise, and then call during those brief moments of quiet.

Finally, I'd like to look at some practical applications. Perhaps the most striking example comes from marine research. Healthy coral reefs are remarkably noisy places, full of the clicks, grunts and whistles of fish and other creatures. Damaged reefs, on the other hand, are often almost silent. In one experiment, researchers placed underwater loudspeakers on areas of damaged reef and played recordings of healthy reefs. Over several weeks, these areas attracted significantly more young fish than areas where no sound was played. Since fish play an important part in keeping reefs clean, this could help damaged reefs to recover.

Looking to the future, many researchers believe that monitoring soundscapes could become a standard tool in conservation. For example, it could provide a cheap way of finding out whether rewilding projects, where land is allowed to return to a more natural state, are actually working. If the soundscape becomes richer over time, that's a good sign that wildlife is returning.
Next week, we'll be looking more closely at how acoustic indices are calculated, so please read the two articles on the reading list before then.
That is the end of the listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.

soundcheck.t: This is a sound check. Please adjust the volume so that you can hear this voice clearly and comfortably. The recordings in the test will be played at this volume. If you cannot hear this message clearly, check your headphones or speakers now.
